newsitem.title: UK: Gas Interconnector seen changing European markets.
newsitem.headline: Gas Interconnector seen changing European markets.

text.p: Completion of the Interconnector, the gas pipeline connecting the U.K. to Belgium, will fundamentally change European gas markets and may lead to the adoption of U.K. spot prices across the continent, an energy analyst said on Friday.

Michael Clegg, senior associate at Cambridge Energy Research Associates, told a conference that the 20 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year pipeline will give Zeebrugge, the landing point, the chance to become the first European hub for supplying gas from a variety of sources "at a variety of terms and conditions, including prices."
Clegg said Britain's example in opening access to pipelines to gas shippers through the British Gas TransCo system will have an impact on markets elsewhere in Europe.
At present, he said, access is only obtained through negotiated long term agreements.
"The U.K. initiatives on the introduction of gas-to-gas competition throughout the gas market in the U.K. may well be contagious once a physical connection with the continent is commissioned.
"Belgium will be the focus for this change as gas is contracted to flow to the continent at prices related to those determined in the U.K. market," he said.
Clegg said the European gas industry will be affected in several ways once the Interconnector is in place.

In particular, there will be increased pressure from consumers for transmission companies to relax their opposition to third party access. This will be in line with the European Union's aim of removing barriers to gas trade within the bloc.
Clegg also said gas-to-gas competition will spread from Zeebrugge across the continent once the link is in place, especially when a proposed connection from Zeebrugge to Germany is complete.
And because the Interconnector will be reversible, he pointed out that it will allow Britain to be supplied from Belgium at times of peak demand.
Clegg noted that the 20 bcm per year capacity of the Interconnector is small compared with demand, expected to reach 350 bcm in the EU alone by 1998.

"But the options and opportunities that are created by the construction of this link between the U.K. and the continent are so significant that the structure and business characteristics of the gas industry could be irrevocably changed," he said.

Consultant Michael Brothwood, formerly a solicitor with British Gas, told the conference that cross-European cooperation was increasing as more countries move towards ratification of the European Energy Charter Treaty.
This will introduce legal obligations with respect to transit of "energy materials and products", and should increase the pace of introduction of third party access.

The treaty was signed in December 1994 in Lisbon by 49 states and the European Union. It will not come into effect until at least 30 of those states have ratified it in domestic parliaments, and deposited documentation with the Portuguese government.

By last month, he said, seven signatories had ratified the treaty and deposited their documents, a further nine had ratified but not yet deposited the documents, and the Treaty secretariat says another eight will ratify before the end of this year.
The EU also intends to ratify before the end of this year, and the charter's secretariat expects the 30 necessary ratifications to be in place by mid-1997, Brothwood said.
